reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive secretory diarrhoea caused by biallelic SLC26A3 variants affecting the intestinal chloride/bicarbonate exchanger (DRA)
Often presents antenatally with polyhydramnios and dilated fluid-filled bowel loops mistaken for obstruction
Neonates have profuse watery stool that may be misread as urine, with a strikingly high faecal chloride concentration
The biochemical hallmark is hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, in contrast to the acidosis of most other diarrhoeas
A faecal chloride concentration exceeding the sum of stool sodium and potassium supports the diagnosis
Treatment centres on lifelong oral and, when needed, intravenous chloride, sodium and potassium replacement
Adequate early salt and fluid substitution allows near-normal growth and development
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital chloride diarrhoea results from loss of function of the apical SLC26A3 (DRA) chloride/bicarbonate exchanger in the ileum and colon. Failure of this exchanger prevents chloride absorption and bicarbonate secretion, so chloride is retained in the lumen and osmotically drives water loss, producing a secretory watery diarrhoea rich in chloride. Impaired bicarbonate loss into the gut and secondary activation of sodium- and potassium-conserving pathways lead to systemic hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Chronic volume depletion can cause secondary hyperaldosteronism and renal complications if replacement is inadequate.
additionalDifferentials: Pyloric stenosis and other causes of hypochloraemic alkalosis
Microvillus inclusion disease and other congenital secretory diarrhoeas
Laxative-associated or factitious diarrhoea in older patients
additionalInvestigations: Stool electrolytes with measurement of faecal chloride and comparison to stool sodium plus potassium
Serum electrolytes and acid-base analysis demonstrating hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
Antenatal ultrasound review for polyhydramnios and dilated bowel loops
Molecular genetic testing for SLC26A3 variants
Renal function and, where indicated, assessment for nephrocalcinosis from chronic electrolyte disturbance
redFlags: Severe dehydration and circulatory compromise in the neonate from ongoing salt and water loss
Profound hypokalaemia and alkalosis with risk of arrhythmia
Antenatal features misinterpreted as bowel obstruction leading to unnecessary surgery
Renal impairment or nephrocalcinosis from chronic volume depletion and electrolyte loss
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and consistent chloride, sodium and potassium replacement, growth, development and renal function are usually preserved. Inadequate substitution predisposes to growth failure, renal damage and electrolyte crises.
pitfalls: Overlooking watery stool mistaken for urine in a wet nappy, delaying recognition
Interpreting metabolic alkalosis as inconsistent with diarrhoea and missing the diagnosis
Failing to measure faecal chloride, which is the key discriminating test
Under-replacing potassium and chloride, allowing chronic volume depletion and renal injury
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Provide lifelong oral salt substitution with sodium chloride and potassium chloride to replace ongoing faecal chloride and potassium losses
Give intravenous chloride, sodium and potassium replacement during dehydration crises and intercurrent illness
Correct the hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and restore volume
Consider a proton pump inhibitor as an adjunct to reduce stool volume and chloride loss
Ensure adequate replacement to prevent secondary hyperaldosteronism driven by chronic volume depletion
Monitor growth, electrolytes and renal function, screening for nephrocalcinosis
Offer genetic counselling given autosomal recessive SLC26A3 inheritance, with paediatric gastroenterology follow-up
